pages.title: Best Keyboard Layout for Programmers — Symbols First
pages.metaDesc: Code is punctuation with words attached, so the layout question is about brackets. How QWERTY, Dvorak, Colemak and Programmer Dvorak compare.
pages.heroP: Programmers do not type prose, they type symbols wrapped in words. That changes the layout question: the letters are already solved, and the brackets, braces, quotes and operators are what a layout helps or hurts.
pages.tldr: No layout makes you faster at code than practice does. QWERTY keeps symbols where your muscle memory expects them; Colemak moves some letters for comfort but keeps most symbols; Programmer Dvorak rearranges the number row for symbols. Switch only after 60 WPM on QWERTY.

seo.h2: What code actually requires of a layout
p: A rough count of ordinary source code: letters are still the majority of characters, but the shifted symbol row ( ) { } [ ] < > ; : " ' = + - _ / \ | carries a disproportionate share of the awkward reaches, and those reaches are where errors cluster.
So the question is not "which layout is fastest for English" - it is "which layout puts the symbols you type most under the fingers that can reach them without leaving the home row".

LayoutLetter changesSymbol changesCost of switching
QWERTYNoneNone - symbols where every tool, shortcut and tutorial expects themZero
DvorakSubstantial reordering for English comfortNumber row rearranged; brackets movedWeeks of being slower; shortcuts assume QWERTY positions
Colemak17 keys moved; keeps Z X C V in place for shortcutsMostly unchangedWeeks, but lower than Dvorak
Programmer DvorakDvorak lettersNumber row replaced with symbols; digits shiftedHigh - digits need Shift for every number

Programmer Dvorak looks attractive on paper because symbols get the unshifted number row. In practice the digits then require Shift, which is a bad trade for anyone who types numbers - and most code contains them.

For most programmers, stay on QWERTY. The reason is not that it is optimal; it is that every editor shortcut, every bracket-matching habit and every tutorial assumes it, and your bottleneck is thinking, not the 60-70 WPM you already type.

Consider a change only if all three hold: you are past 60 WPM on QWERTY, you type code for several hours a day, and your error report shows the symbol reaches as the main source of mistakes. Even then, expect a month of being slower before any gain.

seo.h2: What helps more than a layout
p:
• Practise the symbols you actually type. Bracket-and-quote drills beat layout changes by a wide margin.
  • Let the editor do the brackets. Auto-pairs, snippets and formatters remove keystrokes; a layout reorders them.
  • Learn five shortcuts properly. Duplicate line, move line, go to definition, rename symbol, format document.
Code typing pools to practise on: Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Rust, Go, SQL. The general comparison is on Dvorak vs QWERTY.

faq.a: Not measurably. It reorders letters for English comfort and moves brackets, which breaks shortcut muscle memory. The evidence for a coding gain is anecdotal rather than measured.
It puts symbols on the unshifted number row, which sounds ideal until you need a digit - then every number requires Shift. For most codebases that is a bad trade.

faq.q: Should I learn Colemak as a programmer?
faq.a: Only if you are already past 60 WPM, type code for hours a day, and want comfort rather than speed. It keeps Z X C V in place, so shortcuts survive better than with Dvorak.

faq.q: What actually makes programmers type faster?
faq.a: Practising symbols, using snippets and formatters, and learning editor shortcuts. Layout changes come last, if at all.
Most sit at 60-90 WPM on prose and 40-55 on real code, because code is symbol-dense. No employer screens for it.

pages.title: Go Typing Practice — Goroutines, Errors, Interfaces
pages.metaDesc: Type real Go: channels, error wrapping, generics-free structs and methods, test helpers. Trains the punctuation Go uses on nearly every line.
pages.heroP: Go is deliberately plain, and that is what makes it a good typing drill: short declarations, braces on every line, := and error checks appear so often that they become the rhythm of the language.
pages.tldr: Go code is brace-dense: every function, block and struct literal opens and closes. Expect 45-55 WPM on real Go even if you type prose at 75; the limiting characters are { } and := on the right hand.

seo.h2: What makes Go distinctive to type
p: Three things. Braces open on the same line as the statement, so almost every line ends with a reach to the right hand. Short declarations (:=) put the colon and equals in sequence, two keys that are not adjacent. And error checks repeat the same three-line idiom constantly, which makes it the single most valuable sequence to automate in your fingers.
The upside is regularity. Once you can type `if err != nil {` without thinking, a large fraction of Go becomes the same motion with different identifiers.

Thirty-six lines of ordinary Go: a package declaration, grouped imports, a struct with a receiver method, an HTTP server start, JSON decoding with the standard error check, context with timeout, a goroutine range loop, a select, slices.SortFunc with a comparison function, sync.WaitGroup, error wrapping with %w, a type switch, a test helper with t.Fatalf, and a mutex with defer.
They are deliberately short. Go lines are short, and the drill should teach the shape of the language rather than test your endurance with a long expression.

Start with the three highest-frequency sequences: `if err != nil {`, `for _, v := range`, and `defer x.Close()`. Type each twenty times slowly, then in a normal round. Automation of those three is worth more than raw speed.
Then add the punctuation that bites: the colon-equals, the ampersand for addresses, and the backtick for struct tags - which needs the key most typists have never used.
Same engine, different grammar: Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Rust, SQL, and Excel formulas. For layout questions, see keyboard layout for programmers.

faq.q: What typing speed do Go developers have?
faq.a: No one measures it formally. Most developers type prose at 60-90 WPM and real Go at 45-55, because braces and short declarations add right-hand reaches.

faq.q: Why is Go slower to type than Python?
faq.a: Go is brace-dense and every block closes with a reach, while Python uses indentation. Go also repeats the error-check idiom, which is fast only once it is automatic.
Yes - 36 lines of ordinary Go covering goroutines, channels, context, error wrapping, generics-era slices helpers, struct tags and tests.
`if err != nil {`, `for _, v := range` and `defer ...Close()`. Those three sequences cover a large share of real Go lines.

faq.q: How long until I see a gain?
faq.a: Two weeks of five-minute daily rounds usually shows 4-7 WPM on Go content, mostly from the brace reach and the := sequence becoming automatic.
